1.5

A. der/die/das

So: Why is this program called der|die|das?

Go back to the beginning of Interaktion 1.5 and find the following nouns. What words do you see highlighted in front of them?

____ Mann

____ Königin

____ Männlein

Each of these nouns — and every other noun in German — has a grammatical gender indicated by the definite article (the word for the) associated with it:

der for masculine
die for feminine
das for neuter.

And these three words, along with their variations for plural forms and various cases, are the most frequently used words in German. (You’ve probably noticed another important feature of nouns in German: they’re always capitalized, regardless of where they appear in a sentence.)

Students often ask: What are the rules for determining if a noun is masculine, feminine or neuter — besides cases of natural gender, like der Mann and die Frau ? Answer: While there are some features that dictate grammatical gender (das Männlein because of the suffix –lein, for example), there are so many rules (and exceptions to the rules) that it’s ultimately more efficient simply to learn each noun with its grammatical gender as you encounter it. Say the article and the noun out loud together; write them together; use them together as often as possible, until you think of them as a unit.

Another basic feature of German is the way verbs change in order to correspond with the sentence subject. This is especially true of the two most frequently used verbs in German, sein (to be) and haben (to have). Most other Germans verbs conjugate by using the verb stem — the part of the verb that remains when the final -en is removed — and adding endings that correspond to the subject of the verb. Here are the stems for some of the verbs you’ve encountered so far:

arbeiten → arbeit–

finden → find–

fragen → frag–

heißen → heiß–

hören → hör–

sagen → sag–

spielen → spiel–

studieren → studier–

B.3

This is how most verbs conjugate in the present tense for ich / du / Sie :

spielen: spiel- ich -e → ich spiele …
du -st → du spielst …
Sie -en → Sie spielen …

A few things to keep in mind when conjugating verbs with du :

  1. If the verb stem ends with -t or -d, you add an extra -e- before the -st , making it easier to pronounce:

    arbeiten: arbeit- du -(e)st → du arbeitest …

  2. If the verb stem ends with -s / -ß / -z , you drop the -s from the -st ending:

    heißen: heiß- du -t → du heißt …
